item.title: Noise-induced Extinction in Hierarchical Food Webs
item.description: arXiv:2611.33569v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Every finite population is eventually driven to extinction by demographic noise, even when the deterministic dynamics have a stable coexistence state. We develop a large-deviation theory of this process for hierarchical food webs of arbitrary size. In a community of $N$ species, the basal species $X_1$ reproduces intrinsically and every consumer may prey on all species below it, so that omnivory is built into the interaction graph. For unit conversion efficiency and self-limitation confined to the basal species, the mean-field dynamics have at most $2^{N-1}+1$ feasible fixed points. We prove that the sign of each passive eigenvalue equals the sign of the extinct species' density in the enlarged community, that every partial community containing $X_1$ is a saddle with one unstable direction for each extinct consumer, and that the coexistence state is the only stable fixed point. A WKB treatment of the master equation gives a $2N$-dimensional Hamiltonian whose fluctuational fixed points are obtained in closed form. The resulting extinction network has $3^{N-1}$ fluctuation-driven transitions, and its coarse-grained dynamics yield an exact recursion for every mean extinction time. We analyse the three-species omnivory module in full, including a minimal set of existence conditions, global stability of coexistence, numerical instanton actions for all nine transitions and the most probable extinction route, which we confirm with stochastic simulations. Finally, we show how deleting a single trophic link reshapes the extinction network.
item.dc:creator: Varun Nevash, Eric Forgoston, M. Ani Hsieh

item.title: The evolution of extreme spatial heterochiasmy in amphibians: interactions between sex-specific meiotic program and chromosome architecture
item.description: arXiv:2611.33634v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Heterochiasmy, sex differences in meiotic recombination, is usually described in terms of genetic-map length, potentially obscuring more consequential differences in crossover location. Amphibians provide striking examples of extreme spatial heterochiasmy, with male recombination concentrated near chromosome ends and female recombination broadly distributed, yet the evolution and genetic basis of this pattern remains poorly understood. Here, we combine a review with a phylogenetic comparative synthesis of male chiasma location across 97 amphibian species. Male crossover localization is phylogenetically structured, and ancestral reconstruction favors predominantly interstitial recombination at deeper anuran nodes, although not conclusively. The strongest correlate of male terminal crossover location is chromosome morphology: telocentric-rich karyotypes retain more interstitial male chiasmata, whereas metacentric chromosomes show more terminal male chiasmata. Genome size and sex-chromosome system show little association. We propose a sequential model in which sex-specific meiotic regulation first establishes a crossover-precursor placement bias, while centromere position influences which precursors mature into crossovers. This model predicts that chromosome fusion, fission or centromere repositioning can alter male chiasma location without requiring changes to the underlying meiotic program. Our synthesis highlights crossover location as a distinct dimension of heterochiasmy with consequences for genome-wide linkage, adaptation, divergence and sex-chromosome evolution.
item.dc:creator: Ezgi Unal, Paris Veltsos, Wen-Juan Ma

item.title: A multi-patch model for sylvatic hematophagous vector dynamics: the impact of landscape anthropization
item.description: arXiv:2611.34735v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a multi-patch model for sylvatic hematophagous vector--(wild) animal interactions with nonlinear migration terms that depend on landscape anthropization. Every patch is a suitable habitat for both animals and vectors, but anthropization reduces the animal carrying capacity and induces animal and vector displacement. We considered three dispersal types. Under unconstrained global dispersal, displaced individuals can move to any other patch. Under the more realistic random and constrained neighbor dispersal, displaced animals move to a neighboring patch chosen either at random or preferentially among less anthropized ones. We parameterized our model for tsetse flies (Glossina spp.) in the districts of Campo, Ny\'e'\'et\'e, and Ma'an, Ocean division, Cameroon. We characterized the equilibria and their local stability analytically for unconstrained global dispersal, and found numerically that, under both neighbor dispersal regimes, populations progressively expand before settling into a stable equilibrium. Under random neighbor dispersal, the effect of anthropization on migration had a much larger impact on steady state densities than its effect on animal carrying capacity. Under constrained neighbor dispersal, populations spread noticeably more slowly, and numerous patches maintained extremely sparse populations. We further investigated invasion speed under different anthropization scenarios. For random neighbor dispersal, invasion times decreased upon introduction of newly anthropized regions, while for constrained neighbor dispersal, anthropized regions either increased or did not affect invasion times. Approximating invasions by pulled traveling waves, we found that anthropized regions act as ``invasion highways'' or ``invasion barriers'' depending on the dispersal type. We conclude that more empirical data on animal dispersal are needed to understand these dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Ivric Valaire Yatat-Djeumen, Lukas Eigentler, Orville Wright Happi-Tchakount\'e, Imma Tcheferi, Pierre Couteron

item.title: Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao Reconstruction of Discrete space Population Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2611.33923v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reconstructing the continuous time dynamics of cell state evolution from sparse snapshot observations can be formulated as an unbalanced optimal transport problem. To study such dynamics at a coarse grained cell type level, unbalanced optimal transport must be extended to discrete state spaces. Inspired by discrete flow matching, we extended the dynamic Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao (WFR) problem to discrete spaces, and derived a closed form for its solution. For particularly large state spaces or more general models, we proposed an unbalanced discrete flow matching as a numerical approximation method, which provides a Markovian reconstruction of the optimal WFR flow. Our discrete WFR framework also stays stable across different coarse grain resolution. Finally, numerical experiments demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed approach, and applications to real biological data supported the plausibility of the reconstructed dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Junda Ying, Xinyu Wang, Peijie Zhou, Lei Zhang

item.title: Statistical survey of the adaptive landscapes of 10,000 antibodies
item.description: arXiv:2606.21351v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Affinity maturation is the Darwinian process by which antibodies improve antigen binding through somatic hypermutation and selection. The adaptive landscape, which defines the set of antibody-specific mutations that improve functional characteristics, has been explored in only a handful of antibodies. Identifying the sites of adaptive mutations in a given sequence, and how these sites vary across the antibody repertoire, can inform the design of therapeutic antibodies. We develop a population genetic framework that leverages the statistics of convergent affinity maturation in B cell lineages sharing similar naive sequences, called public clonotypes, to identify beneficial mutations. Applying this framework to more than 10,000 public clonotypes represented by multiple lineages across 20 healthy individuals, we identify widespread signatures of site-specific selection. We estimate characteristic fixation rates of beneficial mutations across the V gene, distinguishing mutations that are rarely but strongly beneficial across clonotypes, from those that are commonly but only weakly beneficial. The statistics of these inferred landscapes broadly reproduce the rates of convergent mutation in antibodies specific to SARS-CoV-2 and influenza. Finally, we use our framework to benchmark predictions from existing antibody language models, and show that while these models are dominated by non-selective signatures, a simple renormalization procedure can expose signatures of clonotype-dependent positive selection consistent with our predictions.
item.dc:creator: Daniel PGH Wong, Aleksandra M. Walczak, Thierry Mora

item.title: Beyond species-area curves: understanding how diversity relates to area
item.description: arXiv:2609.02365v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Species-area curves, which describe the number of species present as a function of area, have long been used to understand biodiversity and inform conservation efforts. While species-area curves have been studied for a wide variety of fauna and flora, they are often well described by a power law. Theorists have attempted to explain the power law through many mechanisms, including sampling and spatial effects. While species-area curves are informative, they ignore the population sizes of the various species, which is important when considering ecosystem services. Here, we use mathematically rigorous theory and simulations to predict the relationship between the effective number of species from different diversity indices, like Simpson's index and the Shannon index, and area. Using a spatial Moran model previously used to understand species-area curves, we found that when area is sufficiently large, the relationship between the effective number of species, also termed Hill numbers, and area is linear. On the other hand, the relationship resembles a power law for smaller areas.
item.dc:creator: Hwai-Ray Tung, J\'er\^ome Chave, Simon A Levin

item.title: Extending indoor airborne infection risk modelling to 3D, with local surface deposition
item.description: arXiv:2611.13372v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Mathematical models of indoor disease transmission often rely on simplifying assumptions to reduce computational cost. In particular, in the Viral Infection Risk Indoor Simulator (VIRIS)[13], which combines architectural layout, people movement and airborne viral transmission, aerosol concentrations are assumed uniform across room height, allowing a two-dimensional (2D) formulation. Also, particle deposition on surfaces is represented by a first-order removal term acting throughout the computational domain. Here, we extend VIRIS to the VIRIS-3D-L framework to investigate how these two assumptions affect the predicted infection risk. In VIRIS-3D-L, we solve the reaction-diffusion equation in three dimensions (3D), and aerosol deposition is represented by local surface removal through a Robin boundary condition. We compare VIRIS with VIRIS-3D-L across three indoor settings of increasing architectural and people-movement complexity: a courtroom, a care home, and a supermarket. For the courtroom, care home, and supermarket, respectively, at the end of the simulation, the original 2D formulation with global removal predicts average infection risks across individuals of 44%, 78%, and 25%, while VIRIS-3D-L predicts risks of 51%, 85%, and 28%. Thus, VIRIS significantly underestimates infection risk in all three settings. The predictions of VIRIS-3D-L also show agreement with a documented courtroom outbreak that was used to validate VIRIS. Although computation time increases by approximately a factor of four on average, simulations remain feasible on a standard laptop, taking between eight minutes and just under 1.5 hours. These findings suggest that VIRIS-3D-L offers a more physically realistic framework for assessing indoor airborne infection risk in indoor spaces without prohibitive computational costs.
item.dc:creator: Neha Bansal, Katerina Kaouri, Thomas E. Woolley

item.title: Functional nestedness of soil nematode communities across Europe: integrating morphological counts and eDNA reads
item.description: arXiv:2611.18819v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: 1. Soil nematodes occupy multiple trophic positions and contribute to key processes in soil food webs. Their communities vary across land uses and environmental conditions, yet it remains unclear whether these differences mainly reflect taxon replacement or nested patterns of taxon occurrence. 2. Here, we analysed two independent European datasets of soil nematode communities, SOB4ES, based on eDNA metabarcoding, and NemEu, based on morphological identification, to examine how genus composition varies across land uses. We partitioned community dissimilarity into turnover and nestedness-resultant components and compared sites under contrasting land uses with those sharing the same land use, while accounting for geographical and soil-related variation. We also assessed matrix-level nestedness, differences among trophic groups and associations between genus composition and environmental gradients. 3. In both datasets, genus turnover was consistently greater between contrasting land uses than within the same land use. Although the differences were modest, they remained significant after accounting for geographical distance and genus richness, whereas nestedness-resultant dissimilarity contributed little to land-use differentiation. These findings suggest that land-use-associated differences in European nematode communities are expressed primarily through changes in genus identity rather than nested patterns of taxon occurrence. 4. The consistency of this result across independently assembled datasets supports the broader relevance of taxonomic turnover for understanding soil biodiversity patterns across European land uses.
item.dc:creator: Giuseppe Nicolosi, Michael Bonkowski, Carlo Febbi, Christian Mulder

item.title: Mutual Linearity in Nonlinear Population Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2611.14501v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Mutual linearity, the persistence of affine relations among stationary observables under arbitrarily strong changes of one transition rate, is known for Markov jump processes and chemical reaction networks. We show that generalized Lotka--Volterra dynamics form a new class of mutually linear systems, even though species can go extinct and attractors can be chaotic. Any change to one species' equation acts on the others as one effective press and keeps all abundances affinely related: piecewise across extinctions, and as time averages on chaotic attractors.
item.dc:creator: Shiling Liang
